Insulin Resistance Explained Simply: What I Wish I’d Known 10 Years Ago As A Type 2 Diabetic

I still remember the day I got my type 2 diabetes diagnosis like it was yesterday. I was 32, otherwise healthy, and my doctor dropped the phrase “insulin resistance” into our conversation like I knew what it meant. He handed me a 20-page pamphlet full of medical jargon, told me to “cut sugar and lose weight,” and sent me on my way. For the next three years, I stumbled through management making every mistake in the book, because no one had ever given me insulin resistance explained simply for diabetes patients like me. I thought it just meant my body didn’t like sugar, and that cutting out candy would fix everything. Spoiler: it didn’t.

Today, 10 years later, my A1c sits steady at 5.7, I take a fraction of the medication I used to, and I’ve helped dozens of fellow new diabetics wrap their heads around this confusing condition without a medical degree. If you’ve ever felt lost when your doctor talks about insulin sensitivity, or wondered why your blood sugar spikes even when you don’t eat sweets, this guide is for you.

First: What Is Insulin Resistance, Anyway? (No Med School Degree Required)

Let’s skip the textbook definitions and use the analogy my diabetes educator finally used to make it click for me: Think of your cells like a busy coffee shop at 8am on a Monday. Normally, insulin is the barista that brings your order (glucose, the sugar your body uses for energy) right to your table (the inside of the cell) so you can use it to get work done. When you’re insulin resistant, the door to the coffee shop is jammed with extra furniture and boxes. The barista (insulin) bangs on the door, but can’t get in, so all the orders (glucose) pile up outside on the sidewalk (your bloodstream).

Your boss (the pancreas) sees the pileup, so they send more and more baristas to help, but the door is still stuck. Over time, the baristas get burnt out, the orders keep piling up, and that’s when your blood sugar levels stay consistently high — which is how most people get diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.

I recognized this pattern immediately when I heard it. For years before my diagnosis, I’d eat a big bagel for breakfast and crash so hard by 10am I could barely keep my eyes open at my desk. I’d crave more carbs to give me energy, eat a granola bar, and crash again two hours later. That’s the cycle of insulin resistance: your cells aren’t getting the energy they need, even though there’s plenty of glucose floating around in your blood, so your body tells you to eat more to get more fuel. It’s not a lack of willpower — it’s a biological problem.

My Biggest Insulin Resistance Mistakes (The Ones That Wasted 3 Years Of My Management)

I wish someone had told me these things back in 2013, so I could have skipped the frustration of rising A1c levels and constant fatigue. Here are the three biggest mistakes I made that made my insulin resistance worse:

1. I thought cutting out candy alone was enough

I stopped eating chocolate bars and ice cream cold turkey after my diagnosis, but I was still eating three bowls of white rice a day, drinking two vanilla lattes with syrup every morning, and snacking on white crackers between meals. Refined, low-fiber carbs break down into glucose just as fast as sugar does, and they spike your blood sugar just as hard. For six months, I thought I was being “good” with my diet, but my A1c climbed from 7.2 to 7.8, and my fasting insulin levels were three times the normal range.

2. I thought only cardio counted for exercise

I started running 5k four times a week, and I lost 10 pounds in the first three months, so I was shocked when my doctor told me my insulin resistance hadn’t improved at all. What I didn’t know then is that muscle mass is your body’s biggest glucose user. The more muscle you have, the more “tables” there are in the coffee shop for insulin to drop off glucose. I had almost no muscle mass, so even though I was burning calories running, I wasn’t fixing the root of the jammed door problem.

3. I ignored sleep and stress entirely

I was working 12-hour hospital shifts back then, sleeping four hours a night, and stressed out of my mind most days. I had no idea that cortisol, the stress hormone, directly raises blood sugar and makes your cells more resistant to insulin. The occasional cookie I felt guilty about was doing way less damage than my chronic sleep deprivation and unmanaged stress. When I finally started prioritizing sleep, my fasting glucose dropped 15 points in a month — no diet changes required.

The 4 Small Changes That Cut My Fasting Insulin By 60% In 6 Months (My Proven Success Steps)

Once I finally had insulin resistance explained simply for my diabetes management plan, I stopped trying to make huge, unsustainable changes and focused on small, consistent habits that actually targeted the root of the problem. These are the steps that worked for me:

  1. Swap 50% of your refined carbs for fiber-rich whole foods: I swapped half my white rice for cauliflower rice, white bread for seeded sourdough, and added one cup of non-starchy veggies (broccoli, spinach, bell peppers) to every single meal. Fiber slows down how fast carbs break down into glucose, so you don’t get those huge spikes that make your pancreas pump out extra insulin. I also started eating 10 almonds 15 minutes before every meal, which cut my post-meal glucose spikes by 30% for me.
  2. Add 2 20-minute strength training sessions a week: You don’t need a gym membership or heavy weights for this. I started with bodyweight squats, wall push-ups, and 2lb dumbbell curls I did in my living room while watching TV. After three months, I gained 4 pounds of muscle, and my post-meal glucose levels were 25% lower on average, even when I ate the same meals.
  3. Set a sleep and stress baseline: I cut out caffeine after 2pm, started a 10-minute bedtime wind-down routine with no screens, and added a 5-minute deep breathing break every two hours at work to lower my cortisol levels. This small change made a bigger difference in my fasting insulin levels than any diet change I made in the first three years.
  4. Track your fasting insulin, not just blood glucose: Most diabetics only get their A1c and fasting glucose tested, but fasting insulin is the first sign of worsening insulin resistance. Normal fasting insulin levels are under 10 uIU/mL, and mine was 28 when I started testing. Now it’s 11, almost in the normal range. I ask my doctor to test my fasting insulin every three months to track my progress, instead of just waiting for my A1c to go up to know something is wrong.

My Exact 1-Day Sample Routine For Insulin Resistance

If you’re not sure where to start, this is the routine I follow most days that keeps my levels steady:

  • 7am: Wake up, 5 minutes of box breathing, drink a glass of water with lemon
  • 7:30am: Breakfast: 2 eggs, 1 slice of seeded sourdough, 1 cup of sautéed spinach, ½ avocado
  • 10am: Snack: 1 small apple + 10 unsalted almonds
  • 12:30pm: Lunch: Grilled chicken salad with ½ cup quinoa, 2 cups mixed greens, ½ cup roasted broccoli, olive oil and balsamic dressing
  • 3pm: Snack: 1 hard-boiled egg + 1 small orange
  • 6:30pm: Dinner: Baked salmon, ½ cup mashed cauliflower, 1 cup roasted asparagus
  • 8pm: 10 minute stretching routine, no screens after 9pm
  • 2x a week: 20 minute bodyweight strength training session right after dinner

Common Questions (FAQ) About Insulin Resistance For Diabetics

I get these questions every week from fellow diabetics who are just learning about insulin resistance, so I wanted to answer the most common ones here:

1. Can you reverse insulin resistance if you already have type 2 diabetes?

From my personal experience and what my care team has told me, yes, for many people, especially if you catch it early. I’m 10 years into my type 2 diagnosis, and I cut my fasting insulin levels by 60% with consistent small changes. It doesn’t work for everyone, and it’s not a “cure” for diabetes, but most people see significant improvements with targeted lifestyle changes. Always work with your doctor before adjusting your medication or management plan.

2. Do I need to cut out all carbs to fix insulin resistance?

Absolutely not! I tried keto for two months, and I was miserable, my cholesterol went up, and I had no energy to exercise. You don’t need to cut out carbs entirely — you just need to choose high-fiber, whole grain carbs, portion them correctly, and pair them with protein and fat to slow down glucose absorption. I still eat fruit, sourdough, and quinoa regularly, I just avoid large portions of refined white carbs like white bread, white rice, and pastries.

3. How do I know if I have insulin resistance, other than blood tests?

The most common signs I had were: extreme fatigue after meals, constant cravings for sugar or carbs, weight gain around your midsection that’s hard to lose, frequent urination, and regular brain fog. If you have two or more of these symptoms, ask your doctor to test your fasting insulin levels next time you get blood work done, not just your fasting glucose. Insulin resistance often shows up in insulin levels years before your blood glucose starts to rise.

4. Will medication fix insulin resistance on its own?

I was on metformin for four years, and it helped lower my blood sugar a little, but it didn’t fix the root of my insulin resistance. Medication is a helpful tool, but it’s not a replacement for diet, exercise, and sleep changes. I still take a low dose of metformin today, but my insulin levels only improved once I added the lifestyle habits I shared above.

Final Thoughts + Free Resource For You

Having insulin resistance explained simply for diabetes patients changed my entire management journey, and I hope it’s changed yours too. You don’t need to make huge, overwhelming changes all at once — start with one small step this week, like adding a cup of veggies to your dinner, or taking 5 minutes to stretch before bed. Small consistent changes add up faster than you think.
